title: Assumption of Moses

stories.title: 📜 Assumption of Moses
summaryBullets: Moses, near death, appoints Joshua as his successor and entrusts to him the books he must preserve until God’s visitation (chapters 1–2).
He outlines Israel’s history: future idolatry, captivity, and restoration under divine guidance (chapters 3–5).
Moses speaks of coming tyrants and persecutions, including references that may point to the Hasmonean and Herodian rulers (chapter 6).
A faithful Levite named Taxo and his seven sons choose death over violating God’s law amid persecution (chapter 9).
Moses comforts Joshua, affirming God’s established covenant and promising ultimate vindication (chapters 11–12).
crossRefs: Jude 1:9: Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not dare bring a railing judgment against him but said, The Lord rebuke you; Origen names a book called the Ascension of Moses as the place Jude took that account from.

Deuteronomy 34:5-6: Moses dies in the land of Moab and the LORD buries him in the valley opposite Beth-peor, and no man knows his grave to this day, which is the silence a dispute over his body is filling.
Zechariah 3:1-2: Satan stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him, and the answer comes, The LORD rebuke you, O Satan, which is word for word what Jude puts in Michael's mouth.

Deuteronomy 31:7-8: Moses calls Joshua and charges him in the sight of all Israel to be strong and courageous, because the LORD goes before him and will not fail him or forsake him, the handover this book stretches into an entire work.

Jeremiah 32:14: Take these deeds, the sealed one and the open one, and put them in an earthenware jar so that they may last a long time, the same instruction Moses gives Joshua here about the books he is leaving behind.

2 Maccabees 7:1-42: Seven brothers and their mother are tortured to death one after another under Antiochus for refusing to eat swine's flesh, the nearest surviving parallel to the Levite Taxo taking his seven sons into a cave to die rather than transgress.

Deuteronomy 32:35-36: Vengeance is mine and recompense, for the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants, the promise the hymn in this book turns into a scene with the Most High rising from his throne.

Hebrews 8:6: Christ has obtained a more excellent ministry as the mediator of a better covenant, established on better promises, the office this book claims for Moses in the line a fifth-century writer quoted when he identified the work by name.

translationNotes.note: Jude 1:9 reports that Michael the archangel disputed with the devil over the body of Moses and would not bring a railing charge, saying only, The Lord rebuke you. Origen, in On First Principles 3.2.1, written between about AD 220 and 230, states that Jude took the account from a small book called the Ascension of Moses. Deuteronomy 34:5-6 says the LORD buried him in a valley in Moab and no man knows his grave. The surviving manuscript cannot supply the dispute: it breaks off in the middle of chapter 12, before Moses dies at all.

The words are not new with Jude. Zechariah 3:1-2 has Satan standing at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him, and the answer comes back, The LORD rebuke you, O Satan. Jude puts the identical sentence in Michael's mouth, and the verses around it in Jude are about men who blaspheme whatever they do not understand.

The whole work survives in one incomplete copy, and that copy is an erased undertext. A palimpsest is a parchment scraped clean and written over because parchment cost too much to throw away, and the earlier writing can often still be read underneath it. This one sits in codex C 73 inf. at the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan, written in Latin in the sixth century. Antonio Maria Ceriani found it and published it in 1861. Roughly a third of the text is gone, the ending included.

A farewell speech given by a dying man to his heirs, and a fixed shape in this literature: he gathers them, reviews the past, tells them what is coming, presses a charge on them, and dies. Genesis 49 is the model, where Jacob calls his sons to tell them what will befall them in the last days. Deuteronomy 33 and Joshua 23-24 do the same for Moses and for Joshua, and Acts 20:17-38 has Paul do it at Miletus for the elders of Ephesus.

translationNotes.term: Oil of cedar and earthen vessels
translationNotes.note: Moses charges Joshua to set the books in order, anoint them with oil of cedar and put them away in earthen vessels in the place God made from the beginning of the world. Cedar oil was used on papyrus and parchment to keep insects and rot out of it. Jeremiah 32:14 gives the same practice as a direct command, to put the deeds in an earthenware jar so that they may last a long time. It is how the Dead Sea Scrolls survived.

Chapter 9 turns aside to a Levite named Taxo who takes his seven sons into a cave and tells them to die rather than transgress the commandments. What the name means has never been established. 2 Maccabees 7:1-42 holds the closest surviving parallel: seven brothers and their mother put to death one at a time under Antiochus for refusing swine's flesh, each of them speaking before he dies.

A man of the tribe of Levi, the one tribe given no territory of its own. Numbers 18:20-24 assigns the Levites the tithe in place of land, because the LORD is their inheritance, and Numbers 3:5-10 sets them to serve the priests and keep the charge of the tabernacle. Calling Taxo a Levite places him in the tribe set apart for the sanctuary and holding no stake in the ground.

The Latin hymn in chapter 10 opens with the line that then zabulus will have his end. Zabulus is a worn-down spelling of diabolus, the Greek diabolos brought into Latin, which means slanderer or false accuser. Romans 16:20 makes the same promise, that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet, and Revelation 20:10 gives the end of the devil.

Chapter 6 describes a king who is not of priestly descent, insolent and reckless, who reigns thirty-four years, kills the chief men and is followed by sons reigning shorter terms. Herod reigned from 37 to 4 BC, was not of the priestly line, and left a kingdom his sons divided between them. Under the Hasmoneans before him the high priest and the ruler had been the same man, which is why not of priestly descent is worth the writer's breath.

Herod's family were Idumeans, the people of Edom, brought into Judaism in the century before him. Edom descends from Esau: Genesis 36:1 says plainly that Esau is Edom, and Genesis 25:29-34 gives the sale of the birthright for a bowl of stew. Numbers 20:14-21 has Edom refuse Israel passage through his land, and Obadiah 1:10-14 charges Edom with standing across the way while Jerusalem was sacked.

translationNotes.term: The powerful king of the west
translationNotes.note: Chapter 6 ends with a mighty king from the west who takes captives and burns part of the temple with fire. Publius Quinctilius Varus, Roman governor of Syria, put down the rising that followed Herod's death in 4 BC, and that revolt was crushed with mass crucifixions. The campaign is how the date of the finished book is fixed to the early first century AD.

Rome used it on slaves, rebels and provincials, in numbers, where it could be seen from the road. Roman citizens were exempt from it. Deuteronomy 21:22-23 requires a body hung on a tree to be taken down the same day, since a hanged man is under God's curse and the land must not be defiled, and Galatians 3:13 quotes that verse.

The day God comes to inspect and settle accounts, for good or for ruin. Moses tells Joshua to keep the books until it comes. Isaiah 10:3 asks what they will do in the day of visitation, Jeremiah 6:15 sets it as the time they will be brought down, and Luke 19:44 has Jesus tell Jerusalem she did not know the time of her visitation. 1 Peter 2:12 turns the same word toward a day when God is glorified.

One who stands between two parties and makes the agreement hold. The line that identified this book says God prepared Moses before the foundation of the world to be the mediator of his covenant, and it stands in the text at the end of chapter 1. Galatians 3:19 says the law was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator, 1 Timothy 2:5 says there is one mediator between God and men, and Hebrews 8:6 calls Christ the mediator of a better covenant.

Ancient book lists usually gave a line count beside each title. A stichos was a standard measured line, and scribes were paid by the count and used it to check whether a copy had dropped anything. The Stichometry of Nicephorus is a list of that kind, and it names a Testament of Moses and an Assumption of Moses as two separate books, which is why modern editions print this text under either name.

The book turns from history to a song: God's kingdom appears throughout his creation, the adversary comes to his end and sorrow goes with him, the Most High rises from his throne, the earth trembles and the sun goes dark, and Israel is lifted up to the stars. Daniel 12:3 has the wise shine like the brightness of the sky and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars. Revelation 21:4 has every tear wiped away and death and mourning gone.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses delivers prophetic farewell instructions to Joshua, recounting Israel’s future trials, faithful remnant, and God’s ultimate vindication.

intro:
The Assumption of Moses, also printed as the Testament of Moses, is a farewell address. Moses, in the last year of his life, hands his testimony to Joshua son of Nun, charges him to preserve the books until the day of God's visitation, and then recites Israel's history forward from the entry into the land: the settlement and the kingdom, the sin that brings captivity, the return, the corruption of the priesthood, a persecution under which men are forced to blaspheme, and the vindication that follows. Chapter 9 turns aside to a Levite named Taxo who takes his seven sons into a cave and tells them to die rather than transgress the commandments. Chapter 10 answers with a hymn: God's kingdom appears throughout His creation, Satan is no more, the Most High rises from His throne, and Israel is lifted to the stars. Joshua then protests that he cannot bury Moses or lead the people, and Moses answers him. The text breaks off in the middle of that answer, in chapter 12.

The whole work survives in one incomplete copy. It is the erased undertext of palimpsest leaves in codex C 73 inf. of the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan, written in Latin in the sixth century, and Antonio Maria Ceriani found it there and published it in 1861 in his Monumenta sacra et profana. Roughly a third of the text is gone, including the ending. The Latin is a translation from Greek; R. H. Charles argued in his 1897 edition that a Hebrew original stood behind the Greek. No Greek or Semitic copy has been found. The manuscript carries no title. Ceriani identified it as the lost Assumption of Moses because Gelasius of Cyzicus, writing in the fifth century, quotes a line that ascribes to Moses that God prepared him before the foundation of the world to be the mediator of His covenant, and attributes that line to the book of the Assumption of Moses. The line stands in this text at 1:14. Ancient canon lists, among them the Stichometry of Nicephorus, name a Testament of Moses and an Assumption of Moses as two separate works, and Charles proposed that the surviving text is the Testament and that the Assumption was a distinct book later joined to it. Modern editions therefore print it under either name.

Jude 1:9 reads, "But even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, 'The Lord rebuke you!'" Origen, in On First Principles 3.2.1, written between about AD 220 and 230, states that Jude's account of Michael and the devil disputing over the body of Moses is taken from a small treatise called the Ascension of Moses. Those are the two fixed points: Jude reports the dispute, and Origen names a book by that title as the source Jude drew on. What the manuscript cannot establish is that this Latin text is that book. It breaks off before Moses dies, and no surviving leaf carries any dispute over his body.

The date comes from chapter 6, which describes an insolent king who is not of priestly descent, who rules thirty-four years, kills the chief men, and is followed by children who reign for shorter periods; then a powerful king of the west comes, takes captives, and burns part of the temple with fire. Herod reigned from 37 to 4 BC, was not of priestly descent, and was succeeded by sons who divided his kingdom; Varus, the Roman governor of Syria, put down the revolt that followed Herod's death in 4 BC, in a campaign in which fire took part of the temple and rebels were crucified. The final form of the book therefore belongs to the early first century AD. No communion receives it as canonical.
